speaker: Maya
text: Grab the episode sheet. Three boxes: maize, Iroquois Confederacy, pristine wilderness. Circle the ones you couldn't explain right now — eight minutes, you'll check all three off. And start here: around 1100, a city on the Mississippi rivaled medieval London. No wheels, no horses, no written language.

speaker: Marcus
text: Four topics, three boxes, and it all gets you ready for one kind of question: two societies, side by side. What's different, and why.

speaker: Marcus
text: First: the environment wrote the rules for Native societies in North America. Same continent, totally different lives, and most of it comes down to the land.

speaker: Maya
text: Same continent, totally different lives? Give me the extremes.

speaker: Marcus
text: Start with the Southwest. Hot, dry, unforgiving. The Pueblo peoples built adobe villages and farmed the desert — irrigation, careful water management. Corn, beans, and squash out of dry ground. That took real engineering, and it's why they could stay in one place.

speaker: Maya
text: Farming the desert is impressive. But not everybody farmed — the Plains were nomads, right?

speaker: Marcus
text: The Plains, yes. Open grassland, enormous bison herds. No horses yet — those arrive with the Spanish — so people followed the herds on foot, lived in portable tipis, and moved with the seasons.

speaker: Maya
text: And the Northeast? Longhouses, wooden walls?

speaker: Marcus
text: Woodlands, rivers, coastline. Towns ringed by wooden walls, longhouses holding whole extended families. Corn in summer, hunting and fishing the rest of the year.

speaker: Maya
text: Hold on. When I hear "Native American," my brain pictures one thing. Tipis, maybe. Tell me that's wrong.

speaker: Marcus
text: It's wrong, and it's exactly the mistake most people walk in with. There was never one Native culture. Same as asking if there's one European culture. Environment decides food. Food decides whether you move or stay. And that decides how you live.

speaker: Maya
text: Okay, one box I can actually check.

speaker: Marcus
text: Check it. But these societies were not isolated from each other. Turquoise mined in the Southwest turns up in temples deep in Mesoamerica. Copper from the Great Lakes travels east of the Mississippi.

speaker: Maya
text: How far is that? Half a continent?

speaker: Marcus
text: Hundreds of miles, yes. Shell from the Gulf Coast moves inland too. So these were not isolated tribes. They were connected by trade across the whole continent. And sitting at the center of it was Cahokia.

speaker: Maya
text: I know the name and nothing else. A few huts and some cornfields?

speaker: Marcus
text: Closer to the opposite. Around 1100, Cahokia held maybe 10,000 to 20,000 people, right across the river from what is now St. Louis.

speaker: Maya
text: I got lost in St. Louis once, so I'll take your word on the river.

speaker: Marcus
text: Moving on. At its center, Monk's Mound, an earthen pyramid a hundred feet tall, built basketful by basketful. At its peak, it rivaled or exceeded medieval London.

speaker: Maya
text: Rivaled London? In 1100? Seriously?

speaker: Marcus
text: The estimates put it right up there. It happened with no wheels and no horses and no written language. Maize made the scale possible. Native farmers in Mesoamerica bred maize from a wild grass called teosinte, over thousands of years. They didn't find this crop. They built it.

speaker: Maya
text: They invented corn? From scratch?

speaker: Marcus
text: From a grass, over thousands of years. Then it traveled north century by century, and everywhere it arrived, populations grew and towns got bigger. No maize, no extra food. No extra food, no Cahokia.

speaker: Maya
text: And then it just emptied out? By the mid-1300s?

speaker: Marcus
text: Around then. Why is one of the real mysteries. Could be environmental, could be political, probably both. Nobody's fully sure.

speaker: Maya
text: How do we know any of this? The city is gone.

speaker: Marcus
text: The mounds are still there. Archaeology fills in the rest: burials, trade goods, the city layout. Plus early French explorers who saw the mounds and recorded them. Now, a city that big needs a government. Which brings us to the second box, and the Iroquois and the Pueblo solved that problem in opposite ways.

speaker: Maya
text: Okay, Iroquois Confederacy, Grand Council, everybody agrees... so did they have, like, a president? No, that's me turning it into America. But somebody was in charge, right?

speaker: Marcus
text: Not the way you're picturing. The Iroquois bound five nations together under the Great Law of Peace, with a Grand Council where everyone had to agree. Clans traced through the mother's line chose the council leaders, and no nation could be dragged into a war it hadn't voted for.

speaker: Maya
text: Five nations and everybody has to agree? How did anything get done?

speaker: Marcus
text: Slowly. But it held for centuries. Now compare that to the Pueblo world, which was village-based. Each adobe town largely ran its own affairs, tied to its neighbors by trade and ceremony, with the kiva, the underground ceremonial room, at the center of it all. One side builds a multi-nation confederacy, the other keeps it local. Different land, different problems, so different governments. There's your whole answer: two differences.

speaker: Maya
text: I've heard people connect the confederacy to American federalism. Is that real?

speaker: Marcus
text: Some historians think so. Others say it's overstated, and I don't think that's settled. What nobody disputes is that the Iroquois had a working federal system while most of Europe was still run by kings.

speaker: Maya
text: Two down. Okay, topic three. This one I'm actually sure about. Native peoples lived in harmony with nature. Took what they needed, left no trace, didn't really change anything. The corn thing, sure, but that's farming, that's different.

speaker: Marcus
text: Half of that holds. They knew their land really well. The "no trace" part is where it falls apart — and farming is where it starts, not an exception to it.

speaker: Maya
text: Come on. Planting corn is not the same as clear-cutting a forest.

speaker: Marcus
text: They did both. Controlled burns to clear brush and flush out animals for hunting. Forests cleared for fields, on a massive scale. Traps built across rivers to catch fish.

speaker: Maya
text: Okay, that's not "harmony." That's landscaping.

speaker: Marcus
text: The historian William Cronon made the case in Changes in the Land: what Europeans called wilderness was a landscape people had been working for centuries. And it looked empty partly because epidemics had already swept through and emptied villages before most Europeans ever saw the interior.

speaker: Maya
text: So in a lot of places, by the time Europeans show up, they're walking into a post-apocalypse and calling it Eden.

speaker: Marcus
text: That's the debate to remember: pristine wilderness, or a land people engineered? The evidence is on one side.

speaker: Maya
text: One world down. The collision, Europe sailing into this world, is next time. Three boxes, let's land them. One: environment shaped Native societies. Go.

speaker: Marcus
text: Mostly the chain from the top. Southwest farms, Plains hunts, Northeast does both.

speaker: Maya
text: Checking that one.

speaker: Maya
text: Two was Iroquois versus Pueblo. Confederacy against... little independent towns?

speaker: Marcus
text: Villages, yes, loosely tied by trade and ceremony. Don't drop that part. Five nations versus town councils.

speaker: Maya
text: Checking that one too.

speaker: Maya
text: Three: pristine wilderness, true or false.

speaker: Marcus
text: False. They cleared it and planted it.

speaker: Maya
text: And that's the third.

speaker: Maya
text: Two questions, AP-shaped. Say your answer before I give it. One: name one big difference between how the Iroquois and the Pueblo ran things.

speaker: Maya
text: Iroquois: multi-nation confederacy with a consensus council. Pueblo: independent village councils. Two differences, one line each.

speaker: Maya
text: Two: what made Cahokia possible, and why?

speaker: Maya
text: Maize. Bred from teosinte, carried north over centuries. No maize, no Cahokia.

speaker: Maya
text: Check your three boxes. Episode one in the books. Next time: why Europe finally sailed west. For gold, for God, and for—

speaker: Marcus
text: Mostly gold.
